sources.name: RunRepeat, Runner's percentile calculator (5K men's table)
sources.measures: Chip or gun finish time of male finishers in timed road 5K races, all ages pooled; percentile table where the 1st percentile is the fastest 1%. Dataset described as '35 million results collected in the last 20 years from more than 28,000 races'; races and countries not named, methodology not described.
sources.notes: Values converted here only from h:mm:ss to seconds for the values field; as published: 1st 00:17:30, 10th 00:23:26, 20th 00:26:04, 30th 00:27:58, 40th 00:29:41, 50th 00:31:28, 60th 00:33:28, 70th 00:35:55, 80th 00:39:21, 90th 00:45:43. Page first published 15 Nov 2017, last updated 1 Mar 2024; the 35M-result pool spans roughly 2004-2024 rather than a single reference year. Author Vania Nikolova. Women's table: 1st 21:39, 50th 37:28, 90th 52:24.

sources.name: RunRepeat with IAAF, '133 stats on 5K running races in the US' (men's recreational percentiles)
sources.measures: Finish times of male recreational 5K race participants in the United States, 2009-2018 (2,616,876 participants in 2018, 1,015,180 men). Percentile table labelled 'men's recreational finish times' is undated. Parkrun events explicitly excluded because timing is not individual.
sources.notes: As published: 1st 17:49, 10th 22:06, 20th 24:38, 30th 26:48, 40th 28:56, 50th 31:18, 60th 34:15, 70th 38:17, 80th 44:24, 90th 53:22. Mean given here is the 2018 men's average of 35:22 (men's average rose from 32:12 in 2009). Same organisation and compiler (Vania Nikolova) as the percentile calculator, so not an independent dataset; the two RunRepeat tables disagree on p1 (17:49 vs 17:30) and p90 (53:22 vs 45:43). Also lists 'American recreational 5k record: 15:37' (2018).

sources.name: Outside Run, 'What's a Good 5K Time? Here's What the Latest Data Says'
sources.measures: 2.2 million individual finish times gathered by the author from US 5K road races in 2024; medians, 25th/75th percentiles and top-5%/top-10% cutoffs by sex and age group. Overall men's median only; no overall men's top 10% or top 1%.
sources.notes: Men's overall median 32:00 (women 39:00, all 36:00). By age group, men's top 10% cutoffs: 15-18 19:10, 19-22 20:09, 23-29 20:09, 30-39 22:13, 40-49 23:05, 50-59 24:11, 60-69 25:28, 70-79 28:06; top 5%: 15-18 18:03, 23-29 18:14, 30-39 20:19, 40-49 21:14. Only 1.85% of all results (41,150) were under 20:00, both sexes combined. Article updated 15 Apr 2026, no author named, raw data not published; included as the only independent large-sample check on the RunRepeat median.

definition: Chip or gun finish time of male finishers in timed road 5K races, all ages pooled; percentile table where the 1st percentile is the fastest 1%. Dataset described as '35 million results collected in the last 20 years from more than 28,000 races'; races and countries not named, methodology not described.
caveat: No national statistics office, peer-reviewed paper or parkrun publication gives a men's 5K percentile table; the top-1% figure rests on RunRepeat's aggregated race-result pool, which does not name its races, countries or method. RunRepeat's two tables put the fastest 1% of male 5K race finishers at 17:30 (global calculator, updated 2024) and 17:49 (US 2009-2018 page), and both derive from the same organisation. The population is self-selected timed race finishers, all ages pooled, not men in general; the 2024 US sample from Outside Run says fewer than 2% of all finishers broke 20:00, which is consistent with a men's top-1% mark in the 17-18 minute range. parkrun data is excluded from RunRepeat's US figures. The question gives no country, so the global calculator table is the primary match.

sources.measures: Finish time of half marathon finishers, all ages pooled, in a percentile table where the 1st percentile is the fastest 1%. sources.name: Outside Run (Outside Online), 'What's a Good Half Marathon Time? Here's What the Latest Data Says' (author's compilation of 2024 US race results)
sources.measures: Finish times of about one million half marathon finishers in races across the United States in 2024, compiled by the article's author (data resource runningwithrock.com). Reports median by sex, and median, 25th/75th percentile, top 10% and top 5% thresholds by sex and ten-year age group (20-29 to 70-79). No top 1% figure.
sources.notes: Published 24 Sep 2025, updated 19 Jan 2026. Overall median stated only as 'about 2:13' (7980 s here is that rounded figure). Men's median 2:03:28, women's 2:21:42. n is the sum of the published age-group counts (men 548,270; women 618,015), ages 20-79 only. Top 10% by age group, men: 20-29 1:33:57, 30-39 1:34:31, 40-49 1:37:21, 50-59 1:42:25, 60-69 1:48:25, 70-79 1:59:33; women: 1:49:42, 1:49:52, 1:52:44, 1:58:13, 2:04:40, 2:20:36. Top 5% men 20-29 1:26:20, women 20-29 1:42:51. Also quotes NYRR half marathon qualifying standards (men 18-34 1:21:00, women 18-34 1:32:00) and says they correspond to roughly the top 2-3% in younger age groups. Journalist-compiled, not peer reviewed; access to the page is sometimes gated behind a login redirect.

sources.name: San Francisco Marathon half marathon results 2008-2021, open data analysis by Debarghya Das
sources.measures: Finish times of 135,944 finishers of the San Francisco Marathon's half marathon events, 2008-2021 (no race in 2020), scraped from the RunRaceResults hosting site. Percentiles published with 99% meaning the fastest 1%.
sources.notes: Keys here follow the site's lower-is-better convention (p1 = fastest 1%). As published: 99% 1:27:52, 90% 1:48:30, median 2:18:01, 10% 2:59:04, 1% 3:44:25. Men (62,623): mean 2:13:55, median 2:10:03, best 1:03:54; women (73,330): mean 2:28:10, median 2:24:25, best 1:10:45. A single hilly race series, so slower than a national pool; personal-site analysis of the race's own results, not an official publication.

definition: Finish time of half marathon finishers, all ages pooled, in a percentile table where the 1st percentile is the fastest 1%. Dataset described as about 35 million results from more than 28,000 races collected over the last 20 years, across all distances; races, countries and timing method (chip vs gun) not named; methodology not described. Author Vania Nikolova.
caveat: The only source that publishes a top 1% (fastest 1%) threshold for a large multi-race pool is RunRepeat (1:23:59 all finishers, 1:18:37 men, 1:35:55 women), and its methodology, race mix, countries and exact years are undisclosed; the pool spans about 20 years rather than one reference year and is likely US-heavy, so it is not a true world population. The 2024 US compilation reported by Outside stops at the top 5% and gives a slower overall median (about 2:13 vs 2:14:59), and a single race (San Francisco) puts its fastest 1% at 1:27:52, so a top 1% near 1:24-1:28 for mixed-sex finishers is consistent across sources. No national statistics office or peer-reviewed study publishes half marathon finish-time percentiles for all finishers; the question did not specify sex, country or age, so the combined-sex, all-ages figure is the match.

sources.name: RunRepeat: Compare Running Finish Times (runner percentile calculator), female 10K table
sources.measures: Official chip or gun finish times of female finishers in timed 10K road races, pooled across all ages, taken from race results RunRepeat collected. p1 is the time that only the fastest 1% of female finishers beat.
sources.unit_as_published: hh:mm:ss (published as 00:41:12 etc.); converted here to seconds only because the schema needs numbers. Published values: p1 00:41:12, p10 00:53:35, p20 00:58:01, p30 01:01:02, p40 01:03:50, p50 01:06:54, p60 01:10:38, p70 01:15:36, p80 01:22:46, p90 01:33:14
sources.notes: Percentiles are counted from the fast end, so p1 is the top 1% and p90 is the slow tail. The page says its results come from '35 million results collected in the last 20 years from more than 28,000 races' across 5K, 10K, half and marathon. It does not give a 10K-only or female-only count, or exact years. It was first published on 15 Nov 2017 and updated on 1 Mar 2024, so the reference year is approximate. Some secondary copies of the page show 36:18 as the 1st percentile. That figure belongs to a different table (mixed or male), not the female table. The female table fetched directly from runrepeat.com shows 41:12.

definition: Official chip or gun finish times of female finishers in timed 10K road races, pooled across all ages, taken from race results RunRepeat collected. p1 is the time that only the fastest 1% of female finishers beat.
caveat: Only one source matches this definition (all female finishers of timed 10K races, every age). I could not find a second independent large-sample percentile table for that population. Sources not merged, because their definitions differ: (1) Runbundle (runbundle.com/stats/average-race-times/10k, updated Sep 2026) reports a women's mean of 1:08:44 and medians by age group (20-29 59:42, 30-39 1:00:14, 40-49 1:01:45, 50-59 1:04:54, 60-69 1:10:37, 70-79 1:19:04). Its data is 644,865 results that users entered into its calculators, not race results, and it gives no p1. (2) Running Level gives a women's average of 54:13 for 50 competitive UK races from 2016 to 2020. That field is faster and more selective, and the figure is a mean with no p1. (3) RunRepeat's 2019 State of Running (107.9M results, 1986-2018) gives women's average 10K times by age only. (4) A PeerJ study of the Bolder Boulder 10K (2008-2013, 191,693 performances) splits finishers into sex-specific sextiles, but I could not open the full text to read the cutoffs. Mismatch with the question: these are race finishers, a self-selected group that runs faster than women in general, and the pool is mostly US and UK races. The schema has no slot for a text value, so the published hh:mm:ss times appear in seconds in values and verbatim in unit_as_published.
